A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepContour research despite the changed title and expanded presentation. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical experiments on five scientific GEP datasets, including solver timings, spectral prediction errors, contour sensitivity, and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds partitioning comparisons, resolution-transfer results, distribution-shift tests, and prediction-quality analyses.

M1.justification: The FNO backbone, pooling and MLP prediction head, MSE objective, KDE partitioning, and downstream CI solve are retained. v1 Algorithms 1–2 match v2 Algorithms 2–3. Explicit safety-buffer formulas and suggested fallback checks expand documentation without establishing a changed implemented pipeline.

E1.justification: The five physical domains and their dataset constructions remain unchanged. v2 adds evaluation on parameter ranges extrapolated by 5% and 10% for the Plate and Piezoelectric domains (Appendix G.6, Table 19), extending coverage to mildly shifted input populations.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct gap-threshold splitting and K-means splitting as evaluated alternatives to KDE, using the same ENO predictions and CI solver (Table 17). The five scouting baselines, standalone iterative solvers, MLP, DeepONet, and Scout+KDE comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a distinct train-low/test-high protocol: training at N=12,500 and testing at 25,000 and 50,000 without finetuning, with M=0.01Ntest and KrylovSchur-Scout+KDE as comparator (Appendix G.4). Controlled extrapolation and additional contour-parameter and partitioning experiments further expand the evaluation design. The retained main experiment's budgets and stated splits are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's backbone, FNO-hyperparameter, KDE-weight, and Scout+KDE ablations, v2 tests Nmin/Nmax sensitivity, alternative partitioning rules, resolution transfer, and distribution shifts. It also adds an instance-level computational breakdown and prediction-error versus speedup/miss-rate curves (Appendices G.3–G.8, Figure 7), substantially extending the investigation of mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: The 100-run contour experiment, 10-seed coefficient-of-variation study, and mean-plus-standard-deviation runtime reporting are retained. Figure 7 displays variation across test instances for a new analysis, but no changed run counts, significance testing, or distinct uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Tables 16–20 and Figure 7, including 1.71–2.37× speedups under the new resolution-transfer protocol and degradation under extrapolation. Retained runtime tables are numerically unchanged. Table 1 corrects the Plate/KrylovSchur solver speedup at tolerance 1e-12 from 187 to 1.87, and the unchanged FNO/DeepONet errors are correctly described as slightly different rather than an order of magnitude apart.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 adds a formal operator eigenproblem, bilinear weak formulation, and Galerkin reduction, and explicitly requires Hermitian A and B with B positive definite. v1 presents the matrix problem and a less formal discretization explanation. No new theorem or proof is added; the principal projector, network, and KDE mathematics remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a pioneering learning-guided ENO-plus-KDE contour framework, acceleration across five scientific domains, and speedups up to 5.63× while preserving numerical precision. The additional experiments support these contributions without replacing their central meaning.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the rationale for KDE, explicitly disclaims global optimality, and explains how moderate versus severe prediction errors affect efficiency and coverage. It adds diagnostic and fallback recommendations and potential EDA applications with industrial evaluation left to future work. Its explicit Hermitian focus also removes v1's main-text assertion that the method is universal to complex cases.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies MLP and DeepONet architectures and input encodings, validation-only calibration of local/global contour buffers, 32-point trapezoidal quadrature, and offline label-generation timing. Most training, hardware, software, and dataset-generation details were already present. Exact validation-split sizes and calibrated buffer values remain unspecified, and the data-release promise is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against neural eigensolvers, discussing SpIN, NeuralEF, NeuralSVD, Deep Ritz, PMNN, and STNet in Appendix A.2. It also broadens discussion and citations concerning parallel numerical solvers, neural operators, and chip-design applications. These are substantive literature additions beyond citation-format and bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and problem formulation, reorganizes related work between Section 2 and Appendix A, and expands the method explanations and appendix organization. It also changes the title and author line and adds acknowledgment and impact sections. The restructuring extends well beyond inserting new experimental results.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different document template with running headers and single-column appendices, extensively reflowing tables, figures, and algorithms. It adds the neural-configuration table, Tables 16–20, Figure 7, and a standard CI-pipeline algorithm display. Existing figures and tables are largely retained and relocated, with revised highlighting in the architecture schematic.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the controlled partitioning comparisons and prediction-quality failure analysis better support the design choices and clarify applicability limits. Additional implementation details and correction of the exaggerated FNO/DeepONet comparison also improve assessability. The gain is limited by unresolved documentation gaps: the no-finetuning study increases the target eigenvalue count without explaining how the fixed-length output head accommodates it, and validation calibration lacks split sizes and selected parameter values.
